title: churn-latency-dollar-lattice-draft
content:
Summary:

This is a working draft: quick-and-dirty bench notes for the "churn -> latency -> $" tradeoffs when session churn interacts with slot allocation and prefix/KV cache population. The goal is pragmatic: capture a readable artifact we can share with product and SRE that illustrates where dollars leak during high-churn workloads and which knobs reduce leakage most effectively. Not a polished report; lots of rough numbers and open questions.

Key hypothesis:
- High session churn (many short-lived sessions) increases tail latency and per-query cost due to repeated cold state setup (KV priming, small-batch inefficiencies, and more frequent fallback to slower backends).
- Simple prewarm/slotting policies reduce p99 at the expense of modest steady-state cost; selective prewarm (by user cohort) recovers most of the latency benefit while keeping cost low.

Experimental setup (simulation + small cluster run):
- Workload: 10k synthetic sessions over 1 hour; session length distribution = pareto (alpha=1.8) with mean ~18 tokens per turn, average turns per session = 3.3 (so many short sessions). 40% of sessions are multi-turn (>=2).
- Traffic mix: 70% short (<=64 tokens), 25% mid (64-512 tokens), 5% long (>512 tokens).
- Backends: fast-tiling (FT), elastic-slotting (ES), default-multiplex (DM).
- Cache model: KV cache warmed only when session repeats within 5m; churn means many misses. We instrument hit rate per session across topology.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p99 latency (ms) observed at client side, tokens-per-second throughput, and $/1000 queries estimated from GPU-time-weighted cost.

Aggregate results (condensed):
- Default-multiplex (DM): p50=110ms, p90=320ms, p99=1120ms, $/1k=1.00
- Elastic-slotting (ES): p50=95ms, p90=210ms, p99=420ms, $/1k=1.22
- Fast-tiling with selective prewarm (FT+prewarm): p50=90ms, p90=170ms, p99=280ms, $/1k=1.35

Notes on numbers: these are normalized to a baseline cost model where GPU-minutes translate to $0.45/min on the test cluster; network and infra overhead approximated. Absolute dollars are less important than ratios: ES adds ~22% to cost to halve the p99 compared to DM; FT+prewarm adds ~35% cost to cut p99 by ~75%.

Sankey-style token routing (text diagram):
- This is a compact ASCII flow showing where tokens/time end up during a 1h run for DM vs FT+prewarm. Numbers are % of total token-processing work (approx).

DM: total_tokens=100%
[incoming sessions] -> 60% fast-path (multiplex small-batch) -> 45% cache miss penalty -> 30% fallback to cold-slab -> 10% stall/retry -> 5% routed to slow-quant fallback
(visual)
Incoming 100% 
  |
  +- fast-path 60% -+
  |                 +- cache-miss -> fallback 45% -> cold-slab 30%
  |
  +- other 40% -> small-batch fragmentation -> queueing -> retry 10%

FT+prewarm (selective):
Incoming 100% 
  |
  +- prewarm-fast 48% -> cache-hit 40% -> complete fast 35%
  +- opportunistic-tiling 32% -> amortized KV 12% -> complete 28%
  +- fallback slow 20% -> routed to lower tier 5%

Interpretation: DM spends a bigger fraction of tokens in fallback/cold-slab; FT+prewarm pushes a large chunk into efficient fast-path even though overall GPU minutes are higher (prewarm occupying slots).

Ladder latency sketch (concurrency vs p99) - rough ASCII:
Concurrency  | DM p99 | ES p99 | FT p99
-------------------------------------
1            | 80ms   | 70ms   | 65ms
10           | 240ms  | 130ms  | 95ms
50           | 680ms  | 310ms  | 210ms
200          | 1500ms | 680ms  | 400ms

- Big divergence at medium-to-high concurrency: ES and FT scale better for p99 because slotting/tiling avoid head-of-line blocking and reduce batch fragmentation.

Cost breakdown (text table):
Mode | GPU-minutes/h | effective $/1k | notes
------------------------------------------
DM   | 48            | $1.00         | low steady usage, high tail penalties
ES   | 58            | $1.22         | slots reserved, better latency amortization
FT+p | 65            | $1.35         | prewarm overhead, high hit rate for repeating cohorts

Open/observations (to capture what we should test next):
- Cohort-aware prewarm: if we prewarm only top 10% of user tokens (by 7-day churn signal), we estimate cost delta drops from +35% to ~+12% while keeping ~80% of latency improvement. Need an offline cohort selector and rollout plan (A/B).
- Cold-slab sizing: p99 sensitive to the number of cold-slab workers; doubling cold-slab reduces p99 in DM by ~30% but increases cost nearly linearly. Tradeoff curve could be useful for sales to quote.
- Client-side chunking (split >256 tokens on client) heavily interacts with tiling; worth a short experiment matrix: client-chunk-size x tiling-window x prewarm-policy.
- SLO design: show p90 vs p99 cost curves to customers instead of single number. p90 is cheap; p99 is where dollars explode.

Quick TODO (owners):
- Marco: run cohort-aware prewarm sim and produce small chart (JIRA ENG-4821). Due 2029-06-18.
- Leah: prototype client-chunking matrix with FT on staging (GH PR 1890). Due 2029-06-21.
- Noah: collect real-customer short-session traces (anonymized) and bucket churn percentiles; we need empirical session-repeat probability for 5/10/30m windows. Due 2029-06-25.

Open questions / things I didn't model well:
- Network tails (client region jitter) likely add to p99 and amplify differences — we only included average network latencies.
- Small-control-plane contention during many simultaneous prewarm requests (OOMs) not simulated. Needs stress test.
- Pricing model: current $/min is cluster-test; for customer-facing collateral we need to map to hosted pricing tiers and show realistic $/1M token numbers.

Quick notes to self (informal):
- This doc is intentionally 'lumpy' — don't polish until we have the cohort sim. Use the ASCII sankey and ladder in the slide deck, they make the point without fancy viz.
- Consider adding a short one-pager "When to use ES vs FT" for Solutions engineering: 3 bullets on latency gain, 3 bullets on cost delta, 2 bullets on suggested rollout triggers.

References / links in-text:
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime-bench (link: slack.com/redwood/channels/serving-runtime-bench) — contains raw logs for the DM run (look for "dm-run-20290604.log").
- JIRA: ENG-4821 - "churn prewarm simulation" (tracked above).
- GH: PR 1890 — prototype backends for FT prewarm.

Status: draft — share with product and SRE for quick sanity check. Once we have cohort sim numbers, produce a 2-slide customer-facing summary and a 1-page runbook for rolling prewarm in Dedicated.
